newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, in court brief, denies sexual harassment.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, in court brief, denies sexual harassment.

text.p: - U.S. President Bill Clinton on Thursday "adamantly" denied the sexual harassment charge brought against him by Paula Jones and asked a federal judge to dismiss her lawsuit.
Clinton, in a formal response to Jones' lawsuit, said Jones was motivated by greed and had collaborated with his political enemies in an attempt to damage his presidency.
He said he had no memory of ever having met Jones.

"At no time did the president make sexual advances toward the plaintiff or otherwise act improperly in her presence. At no time did the president conspire to or sexually harrass the plaintiff," Clinton's lawyers wrote.

Jones was a state employee while Clinton was governor of Arkansas. She claimed he ordered one of his bodyguards to escort her to a Little Rock hotel room during a government conference in May, 1991 and then asked her to perform a sex act. Jones says she refused.
Her sexual harrassment suit, filed against Clinton and the bodyguard, seeks $700,000 in damages.
"President Clinton adamantly denies the false allegations contained in the Complaint," his attorneys told the court.
They asked Judge Susan Webber Wright to postpone the discovery process until she ruled on Clinton's motion to dismiss Jones suit.

Clinton's lawyers said Jones lawsuit failed to meet the criteria for a sexual harassment action and offered no evidence to suggest she had been emotionally or financially harmed by the alleged incident.

Clinton's motion said Jones had "thrust herself into the public limelight" by announcing her lawsuit "at a political event sponsored by vigorous opponents of the president, while seated next to an attornrey with whom she had agreed to share the proceeds from any resultant book or film deal."
Clinton's lawyers noted that the last name of a woman named "Paula" was not published in an article in a conservative magazine that discussed Clinton's alleged extramarital affairs.

They said Jones had proclaimed herself as the woman identified only as "Paula" in the article "by joining with long-time political opponents of the president who sought to discredit him and his presidency." The motion did not identify the opponents by name.
Jones acted, according to Clinton's motion, "to maximize her potential to derive economic benefit and simultaneously to harm the president politically."
Gilbert Davis, an attorney for Jones, told CNN that Clinton's denial did not change his assessment that "the evidence is strong as it's been filed."
The White House referred questions about the matter to Clinton's personal attorney, Robert Bennett, who was not immediately available for comment.
